title: The Bus Stop and the Bike Store
paras: The bus stop and the bike store — the hands-on companion to "Planning for a Changing Climate". That made the big argument; this one comes to the scheme on your desk. England; the date's in the written guide.

We frame the climate response at a vast scale — net zero, strategic energy, whole cities. But most of us work on ordinary applications: a barn conversion, a small housing site, an extension, a fifty-home scheme on a town edge. That's where a planner holds small levers the strategic debate overlooks. A bike store by the front door not behind the bins. A bus stop visible from the houses. A roof left clear for solar. A front garden kept as garden. None saves the planet alone, but they're cumulative, shaping how people live for the building's sixty-year life. Get them right and you shift a thousand daily journeys out of the car — every day, for decades.

Two disciplines throughout. Proportionality — scale the ask to the development; a car-club bay on a single dwelling discredits the exercise. And honesty about what planning can require, which is where we start.

title: 2. What planning can, and cannot, require
paras: So — what planning can, and cannot, require. Much of a building's climate performance is set by the Building Regulations, not planning; miss that boundary and you ask for what you can't secure, or duplicate the Regs. Fabric efficiency, heating, ventilation, EV charge points, overheating — all Building Regs. EV charging in new homes with parking has been required since 2022, overheating mitigation since the same year.

The bigger shift is the Future Homes Standard, in force from 2027 with a transition beyond — a step change. New homes must emit at least seventy-five per cent less carbon than a 2013-standard home, with no fossil-fuel heating — a heat pump or heat-network connection, not gas — and on-site renewables, in practice solar over much of the roof. So from 2027 the home is low-carbon by default, and your attention shifts to what the Regs don't cover: movement, place-shaping, greening, water, waste storage, and the layout that makes the low-carbon choice easy.

One exception, often mis-stated. A ministerial statement discouraged local plans from setting energy standards above the Regs — but the Court of Appeal confirmed in 2025 it has no force of law and doesn't override an authority's power to set higher local standards where local evidence justifies it. So a sound, evidenced local policy can still ask more than the baseline. Otherwise, don't gold-plate the Regs case by case; spend your energy on the measures planning owns.

title: 3. Getting there without a car
paras: Now — getting there without a car. The most valuable area a planner controls, because how a development connects locks in travel behaviour for the life of the scheme, and transport is one of the hardest things to decarbonise. The prize isn't banning cars; it's making the walk, cycle and bus the easy choice. On majors, Active Travel England is now a statutory consultee, so active travel carries weight.

The checklist. Walking — direct, safe, overlooked routes to shops, school, stop and centre, along the desire lines. Safe crossings where routes meet roads, no severance. Cycle parking secure, covered, by the front door not behind the bins, to the national standard, with room for cargo bikes. The bus — a stop within an easy walk, with shelter, seat and real-time information, plus bus priority or a service contribution where viable.

Then connections — genuine links into the existing network, permeable, not a cul-de-sac island. EV charging under the Regs, a car-club bay on larger schemes. And layout — front doors onto streets, active frontages, low speeds by design, because design, not signage, changes behaviour.

title: 4. The building and its energy
paras: Next, the building and its energy. From 2027 the Future Homes Standard does much of this, so the planner's role is smaller than assumed — but it matters most on schemes the Standard doesn't reach: conversions, changes of use, everything built before it bites. And the biggest carbon saving of all is keeping and reusing the existing building rather than demolishing it — the greenest building is the one that already exists.

So the checks. Reuse first — retention and reuse of the building and its materials explored before demolition? Orientation — daylight and passive solar without designing in overheating? Solar-ready roofs — oriented, unshaded, able to take panels, now or later? Heat pumps — space for the air-source units, mindful of noise and appearance? Heat networks — where one exists or is planned, connection secured or safeguarded? And no gold-plating — energy asks within an evidenced local policy or left to the Regs, not invented case by case.

title: 5. Water
paras: Five — water, the quiet climate issue. Parts of England are water-stressed, and a hotter climate makes drought and flash flooding worse. New homes meet a baseline water-efficiency standard, but where a local plan justifies it an authority can require the tighter optional standard — a hundred and ten litres per person per day — by condition. And sustainable drainage does double duty: managing flood risk and, through planting, delivering cooling and biodiversity.

The checklist. That hundred-and-ten-litre optional standard by condition where justified. Sustainable drainage from the start — swales, basins, rain gardens — holding and slowing water rather than piping it away. Permeable materials for drives, paths and parking, resisting the sealing of gardens and forecourts. Water butts as standard, rainwater harvesting on larger or non-residential schemes. And drought-resilient, low-water planting that survives hotter, drier summers without irrigation.

title: 6. Waste and the circular economy
paras: Six — waste and the circular economy. Waste storage is the most neglected corner of a layout, and it drives behaviour: hard-to-reach, badly sited or too-small bins don't get used. Design it in — accessible, adequate, no further from the door than the general-waste bin — and you lift recycling for the life of the scheme. With food-waste collections rolling out across England, well-placed storage isn't optional.

The checklist. Designed-in storage for general, recycling and food waste — convenient, or unused. Food-waste storage, and space for home composting where there are gardens. Existing buildings retained and reused where possible, saving embodied carbon. Reclaimed and low-embodied-carbon materials, demolition arisings reused on site. And a site waste approach that designs waste out rather than skipping it.

title: 7. Greening and cooling
paras: Seven — greening and cooling. Green infrastructure is the best-evidenced adaptation measure there is, much of it at this human scale. Trees cool streets that would otherwise bake, planting slows water, and since 2024 most development must deliver a ten per cent biodiversity net gain, which planning secures and must see maintained. The commonest failure isn't the requirement, it's the follow-through — the tree that dies unwatered, the net gain unmanaged after year two.

The checklist. Trees for shade, new and retained, where they shade streets, homes and hard surfaces — secured with the space, soil and, above all, maintenance to survive. Protect what exists: a semi-mature tree can't be replaced by a sapling for thirty years, so keep mature trees and hedgerows. And the net gain delivered well — genuinely additional, secured and managed long-term, not just drawn on a plan.

Then green or brown roofs where they earn their place. Real gardens and permeable planting, not paved over for parking. And greening the streets — verges, street trees, rain gardens and hedgerows built in, not value-engineered out.

title: 8. Designing for a changing climate
paras: Eight — designing for a changing climate. Adaptation is the half of climate action planning has quietly always done: making the homes and places we build today comfortable and safe in the hotter, wetter climate they'll live through — cheap designed in early, dear retrofitted later.

Four checks. Overheating — orientation, shading, ventilation and glazing that keep homes cool; the Regs cover new homes, but it's live for conversions and existing stock. Flood resilience — steered away from flood risk, and where it must go there, made safe with raised levels, resilient materials, safe access. Shade and shelter — trees, canopies and built shade in public spaces, streets and play areas. And future-ready — layouts that can adapt, with provision for future solar, EV charging, heat pumps and cooling.

title: 9. Carbon, counted honestly
paras: Nine — carbon, counted honestly. Where good intentions slide into greenwash. It's a hierarchy, and the order matters: reduce first, then supply low-carbon, then offset the small remainder. Cutting what a scheme emits and embodies — reuse, fabric, low-carbon materials, the measures above — comes before buying it away. Embodied carbon deserves attention on larger schemes, and whole-life carbon assessment is becoming normal.

title: 10. How to actually secure it
paras: Ten — how to actually secure it. None of it matters unless it lands in the permission. The earlier you raise a measure the cheaper it is, so pre-application is where the value is won, before design and viability are fixed. A sound, evidenced local plan policy is the strongest foundation. Conditions secure a lot — the water standard, cycle parking, landscaping, EV charging beyond the Regs — provided each meets the six tests: necessary, relevant to planning, relevant to the development, enforceable, precise and reasonable. Larger or off-site measures — a bus contribution, off-site tree planting, a carbon-offset payment, long-term net-gain management — run through a section 106. And design review and the design codes add weight.

Two cautions. Proportionate — the full checklist is for a major scheme; a householder application needs a light touch, and asking a single extension for a travel plan is the overreach that discredits the agenda. And viable and lawful — every measure lands in the same appraisal as affordable housing and infrastructure, and a condition failing the six tests, or an energy ask with no policy behind it, won't survive appeal.

And the PlanRef view. Reduce first, don't gold-plate, offset last. An offset has its place — funding real, local, additional, monitored reduction, like tree planting or retrofit — but it's a last resort for the genuine remainder, not a line a developer buys to avoid designing properly. A "carbon-neutral" badge on cheap, unverifiable offsets is worth nothing; apply the scepticism you'd bring to biodiversity or nutrient credits — additional, secured, monitored, local, or discounted. On the everyday scheme, a bus stop, a bike store, a shade tree and a reused building save real carbon at almost no cost, while the grand gesture with the green label often saves none. The small, honest measure beats the large, marketed one.

title: Practice points
paras: The practice points, quickly. This is small, cumulative, and yours — touched on every application. Know the Building Regs boundary: energy, EV charging, overheating, and from 2027 the Future Homes Standard — seventy-five per cent less carbon, no gas, solar; don't gold-plate them. But local energy policy survives, the Court of Appeal confirming authorities keep the power to set higher local standards where justified.

Movement is the biggest lever, locking in behaviour for sixty years; water, waste and greening all count; reduce first, offset last. Secure it early and proportionately — policy, six-tests conditions and section 106, scaled to the development, viable and lawful. The precise sources are in the written guide; this covers England, dated there. Standards change, so re-check before relying on any point on a live application.
